candidate_concepts.label: Shortest Path with Exactly k Edges Problem Definition
candidate_concepts.description: Defines the problem of finding the shortest path between two vertices in a directed, positively weighted graph that uses exactly k edges, allowing cycles.
coverage_criteria: The student can state the formal problem: given directed graph G with positive weights, vertices v,w, integer k, find minimum weight of a path from v to w with exactly k edges (not necessarily simple).
The student can explain why simple Dijkstra is not directly applicable and illustrate with a small example involving self-loops.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The problem is introduced at 00:20 and discussed in detail with a drawn example graph at 02:14; the professor explicitly states the problem statement and contrasts it with standard shortest path.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single well‑defined algorithmic problem; checking understanding requires only restating the constraints and giving a simple example, fitting 1–2 questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Dynamic Programming Recurrence for Shortest Path with k Edges
candidate_concepts.description: Presents a DP recurrence D[x,y,k] = min_z ( D[x,z,k-1] + w(z,y) ) with base cases for k=0 and k=1, and derives O(n³k) time complexity.
coverage_criteria: The student can write the recurrence and explain the meaning of each term.
The student can identify the base cases (k=0: 0 if x=y else ∞; k=1: weight of edge if exists else ∞) and reason why they are correct.
The student can analyze the complexity: O(n³k) by reasoning about table size and work per cell.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The recurrence is written on the board at 08:02 and explained step by step; the base cases and complexity are discussed at 11:55–18:05.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The candidate focuses on a single algorithmic technique (DP recurrence) applied to one problem; verifying it requires writing the recurrence, base cases, and a brief complexity argument – about three short questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Layered Graph Reduction for Shortest Path with k Edges
candidate_concepts.description: Shows a reduction: construct a layered DAG with k+1 copies of vertices where edges only go forward one layer; running standard shortest path (Dijkstra) on this graph solves the original k‑edge problem.
coverage_criteria: The student can describe the transformation: create k+1 layers, for each original edge (u→v) add a directed edge from u in layer i to v in layer i+1 (0≤i<k).
The student can explain why any path of length k in the original graph corresponds to a path from the source in layer 0 to the destination in layer k, and why the new graph is acyclic.
The student can state the resulting complexity (e.g., O(k²n²) depending on Dijkstra implementation) and recognise this as a reduction that uses an existing algorithm as a black box.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The professor draws the layered graph at 20:20, walks through an example with four layers, and explains why it becomes a DAG and how Dijkstra solves it; the term ‘reduction’ is introduced explicitly.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is one specific transformation technique; the candidate can be tested by asking the student to sketch the construction for a small example, argue correctness, and mention complexity – fitting within 2–3 questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Backtracking as Exhaustive Search with Pruning
candidate_concepts.description: Motivates backtracking as a systematic method to iterate through all possible solutions while using constraints to prune the search space early, illustrated with a Sudoku grid where the most constrained cell is filled first.
coverage_criteria: The student can define backtracking as a form of exhaustive search that abandons partial solutions as soon as they cannot lead to a valid complete solution.
Using a Sudoku example, the student can explain why choosing the most constrained cell and testing only locally consistent values reduces the search effort.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The lecture introduces backtracking at 35:25 using Sudoku; the professor discusses trying numbers, recognising dead ends, and the advantage of picking a cell with fewest possibilities (the ‘most constrained’ heuristic).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is the high‑level idea of backtracking; it is sufficient to check whether the student can articulate the prune‑and‑backtrack loop using a familiar puzzle – typically 1–2 questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Recursive Backtracking Algorithm (Pseudocode)
candidate_concepts.description: Presents the generic recursive backtracking procedure: maintain a solution vector a[1..k], check if it is a complete solution, otherwise extend by computing candidates S_k for position k+1 and recursively explore each candidate, backtracking when none lead to a solution.
coverage_criteria: The student can write (or sketch) the pseudocode for the recursive backtrack(a,k) function.
The student can trace its execution for a small problem (e.g., generating subsets of {1,2}) and explain the order in which partial solutions are explored.
The student can identify the three customization points (is_a_solution, construct_candidates, process_solution) that must be filled for a specific application.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The professor shows the pseudocode on a slide at 45:59 and walks through its logic; later shows the C implementation at 50:01, explicitly discussing the same structure.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The core algorithm is a single recursive function with a clear contract; checking understanding requires reproducing the pseudocode and tracing one small example – about 2–3 questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Backtracking as Depth-First Search on Configuration Graph
candidate_concepts.description: Explains that backtracking is equivalent to performing depth-first search (DFS) on an implicit graph whose vertices are partial solutions and edges represent adding one element; this ensures complete enumeration if no pruning is done.
coverage_criteria: The student can state the relationship: backtracking explores the space of partial solutions in the same order as DFS would visit nodes in a tree/graph of configurations.
The student can argue why this guarantees that every complete solution is eventually reached (if the search space is finite).
The student can give a simple example, e.g., subset generation, and show how the backtracking tree corresponds to a DFS traversal.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The slide at 48:41 explicitly states ‘Backtracking is really just depth‑first search on an implicit graph of configurations’ and the professor reinforces this by comparing the recursion to DFS traversal.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single conceptual link; testing involves stating the equivalence and justifying it with one example – 1–2 questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Backtracking Customization Stubs
candidate_concepts.description: Details the three functions that must be implemented to adapt the generic backtracking engine to a specific problem: is_a_solution (tests completeness), construct_candidates (lists valid choices for the next position), and process_solution (handles a complete solution).
coverage_criteria: The student can describe the role of each stub and give a concrete example of its implementation for a known problem (e.g., subset generation: is_a_solution ⇔ k==n, construct_candidates ⇔ {true, false}).
The student can explain why separating these concerns makes the backtracking framework reusable.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The stubs are introduced at 52:30 (is_a_solution), 53:18 (construct_candidates), and 54:11 (process_solution); each slide gives a precise contract, and the C code for subsets later shows concrete implementations.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: These are three tightly related but distinct customisation points; verifying understanding requires explaining each with an example – about 2 questions total.

candidate_concepts.label: Subset Generation via Backtracking
candidate_concepts.description: Applies the backtracking framework to generate all 2ⁿ subsets of {1,…,n} by using a boolean array where a[i] indicates membership; the candidates are always {true, false} and a solution is reached when k == n.
coverage_criteria: The student can write the is_a_solution and construct_candidates stubs for subset generation.
The student can draw the backtracking tree for n=3, showing the order subsets are generated and relate it to the binary representation.
The student can explain why this generates exactly 2ⁿ leaves without enumerating invalid configurations.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The mathematical formulation appears at 54:56, followed by a detailed walk‑through of the tree at 58:18 and the full C implementation at 1:03:58.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is one concrete, self‑contained application of the backtracking engine; verifying it requires the student to write the stubs and trace the tree – 2–3 questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Permutation Generation via Backtracking
candidate_concepts.description: Uses the same backtracking skeleton to generate all n! permutations of {1,…,n} by maintaining an array of chosen positions; the candidates for step k are the numbers not yet used in the prefix.
coverage_criteria: The student can write the construct_candidates stub that checks a boolean ‘used’ array and builds a list of available numbers.
The student can trace the generation tree for n=3 and list the six permutations in the order produced by the algorithm.
The student can explain why this approach guarantees each permutation appears exactly once.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The lecture introduces permutations at 1:06:33, draws the tree at 1:09:34, and shows C code for construct_candidates at 1:13:39.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is another self‑contained application of backtracking; checking involves writing the candidate generation logic and tracing the tree – 2–3 questions.

candidate_concepts.label: Bandwidth Problem and Backtracking Contest
candidate_concepts.description: Defines the combinatorial optimization problem: given a graph, find a linear ordering (permutation) of its vertices that minimises the length of the longest edge (the ‘bandwidth’). A naive solution enumerates all n! permutations and checks the maximum edge span.
coverage_criteria: The student can state the bandwidth problem: for a graph G=(V,E), find a permutation π:V→{1,…,|V|} that minimises max_{(u,v)∈E} |π(u) − π(v)|.
The student can explain why a brute‑force search over all permutations is prohibitively slow (Ω(n!·m)) and that no polynomial‑time algorithm is known (it is NP‑hard).
The student can outline how a backtracking solver for this problem would be structured using the same permutation‑generation skeleton, but with pruning based on the current best bandwidth.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The professor presents the bandwidth problem on slides at 1:15:04 and 1:19:05, showing a poor layout with bandwidth 7 and an optimal layout with bandwidth 1, and explains the contest structure.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The candidate covers the problem definition and its connection to exhaustive permutation search; verifying requires defining the problem and sketching a backtracking‑based approach – 2–3 questions.
